t: A typo on the front of the bus, and no software to fix it
s: One of our route signs had an extra L in it. The editing software was long gone. AI read the sign's raw file, found the two bad spots and swapped the letters without disturbing anything else.
x: One of our routes ends at a local college. The lighted sign on the front of the bus spelled the college's name with two L's. It has one. It is a small thing. It is also on the front of a bus, in lights, all day. Why it was not a five minute fix The words on those signs live in a file inside a control box by the driver's seat. Someone builds that file with the manufacturer's software and loads it with a thumb drive. We did not have the software. The manufacturer's records showed our file was last updated in 2021. I gave Claude the operator's manual and asked how to fix the spelling. It walked me through the menus, then told me what I did not want to hear: the fix had to happen in the file, and the file needed the software. The first answer was no I asked whether Claude could just read and write that kind of file, or build me a small program that could. It said no. The manual did not describe how the file was laid out, and it was not willing to guess. Its reasoning was that a guess could produce a file that would not load, or one that loaded and broke the signs on buses that were in service. It told me to ask the manufacturer for the layout, or for a corrected file. It was not the answer I was after. It was the right one. What the manufacturer said I wrote to their support desk. The reply cleared up one thing and added another. Our control box did not use the kind of file the manual described. It used a different one. And if I wanted them to make the change, they would need to work up a quote. A quote, to remove one letter. Getting the file out Earlier I had asked Claude whether a thumb drive could pull the file off the box. The manual said it could. So I did. I came away with two files: the message file and a settings file. Now Claude had the real thing in front of it. That changed its answer. What it found The message file is not text. Open it in a text editor and it is mostly garbage, with route names showing through here and there. Claude read it as raw bytes, which is the only honest way to read a file like that. - The misspelled name appeared twice, and it gave me the exact position of each one. - It looked at the start and the end of the file for anything that looked like a check value. - It compared how the other route names were stored. Each name sat between marker bytes. Nothing stored how long the name was. That last point decided the method. If the file had kept a length for each name, shortening one would have meant updating the length too, and maybe more. It did not. The fix The wrong spelling had seven letters. The right one has six. Claude did not delete a letter. It replaced the seven letters with the six correct ones plus a space. That kept every other byte in the file exactly where it had been. The file was 42,453 bytes before and 42,453 bytes after. Two words changed and nothing else did. A space on a sign made of lights is just lights that stay off. It handed me the corrected file and an untouched copy of the original, in case I needed to go back. I asked about the settings file. Claude read it and said to leave it alone. It held hardware settings like brightness, and no route names at all. Where it falls short - It could not test the result. Claude never touched a bus. It told me to load the file on one bus, look at the sign, and only then do the rest of the fleet. That is the right order for any change like this. - The manual was wrong for our box, and Claude's first set of steps came straight from the manual. The file type was wrong and so was the folder name the box looks for on the thumb drive. I knew the folder name only because I had just pulled the files off myself. - The space is still a character. It is blank, but it is there. On a sign that centers its text, look and see that the name still sits where it should. - This trick has limits. Swapping letters for the same number of letters is about the safest edit there is. Adding a route, or making a name longer, is a different job. That one needs the real software. What I take from this The no and the yes came from the same place. Without the file, Claude would have been guessing, and it said so. With the file, it could look, and it told me what it found and why the change was safe. Keep the original. Change as little as possible. Test on one before you do ten. Try it If you are stuck with an old file and no program to open it, start by asking what is in it, not by asking for a fix. --- Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: River's Rocket Works
s: A rocket game I built for River. Design a rocket, fly twelve missions from first launch to a wormhole, and race the whole family around the solar system.
x: River loves rockets, and Starship most of all. So I built him a space program. Play River's Rocket Works How it works You design a rocket in the workshop, then fly it. There are twelve missions, and they get bigger as you go. 1. First Flight 2. Edge of Space 3. Come Home Booster 4. Orbit! 5. Station Delivery 6. Moon Landing 7. Mars Rover 8. Rings of Saturn 9. Red Spot Rally 10. The Wormhole Run 11. The Rainbow Race 12. Asteroid Blaster There's also a free flight mode for when you only want to fly around. Built for a kid and a grown-up together The game talks. A voice reads out every mission, so a kid who is still learning to read can play it. There's a co-pilot assist that quietly helps with the hard parts, so nobody ends the night frustrated. It works with an Xbox controller, a keyboard or a touch screen, and it remembers your stars in the browser. Finish the missions and there's a certificate at the end. The Rainbow Race This is the silliest mission. A glowing rainbow track circles the whole solar system and you pick your racer. You don't have to earn it. The title screen has a Rainbow Race button that takes you straight there. - River, on a shooting star. - Mom, on her unicorn. - Dad, in a Viking ship pulled by goats. - Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, our white Labrador, in her lace collar. Yes, that's her full name. We call her Justice. What I learned A game like this can carry real ideas. Getting to orbit isn't only about going up. You have to go sideways, very fast, and the Orbit mission makes you do it. A kid who has flown that once has learned something a diagram wouldn't teach. It's one web page built on Three.js. If it runs slowly, try it on a computer before a phone.

t: Putting our buses on the map, live
s: How I turned the GPS units already on our buses into a GTFS Realtime feed, and a live map for the public.
x: Our buses already had GPS units. The locations just weren't going anywhere a rider could see. You can watch a demo of the map with made-up buses, and see the feed behind each one. The format that apps already read Trip-planning apps don't want a custom feed. They want GTFS Realtime, an open standard for vehicle positions and arrival predictions. If you publish in that format, any app that knows the standard can read your buses. So the job was translation. Take the GPS data and publish it as GTFS Realtime. I wrote that in Node.js with the standard gtfs-realtime-bindings library, which handles the compact binary format the standard uses. The hard part was not the map Getting a dot on a map was the easy part. The hard part was trip matching. The GPS knows where bus 12 is. It doesn't know that bus 12 is currently running the 9:45 trip on a particular route. The standard wants the trip, because that's how an app connects a moving dot to the schedule a rider is looking at. Working out which scheduled trip each bus is on, from only its position and the time, took most of the effort. What the validator taught me I submitted the feed to Google. Their validator is strict, and it sent back errors I had to learn to read. One meant it couldn't fetch the feed at all. Others meant my predictions had a bus arriving or leaving a stop earlier than made sense. Each fix made the feed more honest. The live map The second piece is a public map page. It uses Leaflet with OpenStreetMap tiles and refreshes every 15 seconds. It was approved for the City's website. I styled it in the same blue and green glass look this site uses, because apparently I have a type. If you run a small system You may already own the data. The work is in the translation, and the standard is free.

t: Making a Sunfish faster without breaking the rules
s: My tuning notes for the Sunfish: the four sail controls, a few ideas I want to test, and the only class-legal way to rig a vang.
x: I was invited to sail in the Sunfish World Championship, and I want my boat to be as fast as the rules allow. The Sunfish is a one-design class. Everyone sails the same boat, and the rules stop you from buying speed. Whatever speed there is comes from preparation and from how you sail. So I sat down and built myself a full tuning guide, starting from Scott Kyle's well-known guide and everything else I could find. Four controls do most of the work A Sunfish has no standing rigging to adjust. Sail shape comes from four things. - Halyard position. Where the halyard is tied on the upper spar sets how high the sail sits and how much power it has. - Gooseneck position. Sliding the gooseneck along the boom moves the sail forward or back over the daggerboard. This is the main control for helm balance. - Outhaul. Controls how full the bottom third of the sail is. - Cunningham. Tightens the front edge and moves the deep part of the sail forward or back. The simplest tip in the whole guide: mark the boom in one-inch steps where the gooseneck sits, so the setting is a glance and not a guess. As the wind builds, the gooseneck moves back. If the boat keeps trying to turn into the wind, it needs to go back further. The sail is lopsided, and that's useful The mast sits on one side of the sail. So the sail is flatter on port tack and fuller on starboard. In medium wind it barely matters. In light air, don't pull the sail in too tight on port. In heavy air, be ready to ease sooner on starboard. Ideas I want to test These aren't proven. They're experiments, to be tried one at a time against a tuning partner. - Slightly different cunningham settings on each tack to even out that lopsided sail. - Using the Jens rig in light air. It's normally a heavy-air trick to tame the sail, but it may also help the boat point. - Practicing puff anticipation as a drill. Easing the sail just before a puff hits keeps the boat flat. Easing after costs you seconds going sideways. The vang that isn't a vang A vang holds the boom down. The Sunfish never came with one, and the class rules don't let you add hardware the builder didn't supply. A little block and tackle would be illegal. The halyard is already legal, though. After the sail is up, the leftover tail runs through the fairlead on the deck and loops around the gooseneck, then cleats off. That holds the gooseneck four to six inches above the deck and keeps the boom from lifting. I wanted more pull, and my first idea was extra wraps. Wraps only add friction. For real mechanical advantage you tie a fixed loop in the halyard tail and lead the line back through it. That gives a two-to-one purchase made of nothing but rope, which is the same trick the outhaul and cunningham already use. It's still only the halyard doing extra work, so nothing has been added to the boat. If you race, check the current class rules yourself, and ask your fleet measurer before you fasten anything new to the boom.

t: A driving game set on our real bus routes
s: A 3D driving game in the browser built from real route data, real streets and about 40,000 real building footprints. It started as a trolley simulator and kept growing.
x: This started as a trolley simulator and got out of hand in the best way. Play the transit simulator It is a big download, so give it a minute to build the city. It runs best on a computer with a keyboard or an Xbox controller. Real data, not a made-up town The routes and stops come from the same schedule data we publish for trip-planning apps. The streets and about 40,000 building footprints come from the City's GIS data and from public building datasets. So when you drive the game, the turns are the real turns and the stops are where the stops are. It runs in a web browser, built with Three.js. You can drive the trolley or a 35 foot Gillig bus, which is the bus you'd see on the street. The handling comes from real vehicle specs, so the bus feels like a bus. That means slowly, and with respect for corners. What's in it - Xbox controller support, and two-player split screen. - An in-game radio. - A free drive mode with pickups that only make sense in Louisiana: hot sauce rockets, blue crabs, crawfish and a shield made of Mardi Gras beads. - An on-foot mode, so you can step off and walk around. And then Formula 1 showed up My son loves F1, so there's now a Grand Prix mode. It's a five-lap street circuit along the lakefront in an F1-style car. It has the five-light start, a racing line you can switch on, a pause map and a podium at the end. Nobody asked for this. I regret nothing. Why a transit manager is building a video game Partly because it's fun. Partly because a game is the most approachable version of a route map there is. A kid who has driven a route in a game knows where it goes. What's next I plan to film the real routes with a 360 degree camera as reference for the next round of work. It's still in progress, so expect rough edges. The game is my own project and not an official City product.

t: A sailing simulator you steer with your hands
s: A browser sailing game that watches your hands through the webcam. Pick a Sunfish, an Optimist or a pirate ship.
x: I wanted a sailing game I could play with River, where you move your body and not a joystick. We own a Nex Playground, the console that tracks your movement with a camera, and that was the first idea. A web browser and a webcam turned out to be the faster road. How you sail it The game watches your hands through the webcam using Google's MediaPipe hand tracking. You steer and trim the sail by moving your hands in the air, and a small panel shows what the camera sees so you know it's following you. Pick your boat - Sunfish. Quick and responsive. This is the boat I race, so I was picky about it. - Optimist. The little boxy boat that kids learn in all over the world. Slower and very forgiving. - Pirate ship. Slow, majestic and terrible at sailing toward the wind, which is historically accurate and also very funny. Each one sails differently. A Sunfish will point much closer to the wind than a square-rigged ship ever could, and the game holds you to that. Real sailing underneath I didn't want an arcade game with a sail painted on. The simulator works out the true wind and the apparent wind, which is the wind you feel once the boat is moving. It knows the no-go zone, the angle too close to the wind where no boat can sail. There are gauges for wind speed and direction, and telltales to show whether the sail is trimmed right. Eight versions It took eight versions. The first was a flat, top-down prototype. Then it went 3D. Then the pirate ship rendered wrong in three separate ways. Then the camera overlay was mirrored and the wind arrow pointed the wrong way. Each round was me sailing it, saying what felt wrong and fixing that. That's the honest shape of building with AI. The first version arrives fast. The good version comes from someone who knows the subject saying "no, a boat doesn't do that" over and over.

t: A dispatch board for when a driver calls in
s: An eight-week driver rotation in a spreadsheet, plus a one-page board that works out who covers which route when someone calls in.
x: The hardest part of scheduling a small bus system isn't the schedule. It's the early morning phone call when someone is out and every route still has to leave on time. You can try a demo of the board with made-up drivers and routes. The problem We run five routes with hourly trips from 5:45 in the morning to 5:45 in the evening, and nine drivers to cover them. On paper that works. In practice the plan changes the moment one person is out, and whoever is on the phone has to work out the new plan from memory. What I built Two pieces that share the same data. The first is a spreadsheet with an eight-week rotation. It has a read-me page, the driver roster, the daily schedule, the weekly rotation and a call-in quick lookup. Anyone can open it and see who drives what on any day. The second is the dispatch board. It's a single web page that opens in any browser, with nothing to install. - Pick the rotation week and the day. - Tap "Called in" next to anyone who is out. - The board reassigns their route from the extra board. - If the extra board is empty, it falls back to supervisors. - If nobody is left, it flags the route "NO COVERAGE" in a way you can't miss. There's also a custom day mode for the days that fit no pattern. Every assignment becomes a dropdown, and the board warns you if you put the same person on two routes. One button resets the day and another prints it. What I learned The rules were already in people's heads. The work was getting them written down precisely enough for a computer to follow. Who covers first? Who covers next? What happens when nobody is left? Once those answers are on paper, the code is the easy part. I also learned to keep the spreadsheet. People trust a spreadsheet. The board sits on top of it instead of replacing it.

t: Replacing the paratransit spreadsheets
s: A small web app for booking paratransit rides, assigning drivers and producing the reports, built with Node.js, Express and SQLite.
x: Paratransit is the door-to-door service for riders who can't use the regular buses. Ours is small: two or three drivers and somewhere between eight and fifteen rides a day. It ran on spreadsheets. Why the spreadsheets had to go A spreadsheet is fine for a list. It's bad at a schedule that changes all day. Every ride gets typed by hand, and every report starts with counting rows. What the app does - A daily schedule that shows every ride and its status. - A passenger list, so a repeat rider is two clicks and not a retyped address. - Driver assignment for each ride. - Mileage and drive time filled in from Google Maps directions, with a manual override for when the map is wrong. - Reports in the shape our federal reporting needs, and an export to Excel for anyone who still wants the spreadsheet. - A phone view for drivers that shows only their rides for the day. - A tab for the vehicles themselves. Under the hood it's plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser, with Node.js and Express on the server and a SQLite database, which is a single file. The part I'm oddly proud of I didn't have admin rights on my work computer, so I couldn't install Node.js the normal way. The first version ran from a USB drive with a portable copy of Node on it. Plug it in, double-click and the app was running. That let me keep building and showing it to people without waiting on an install. What you won't see here Rider information is protected, and none of it will ever appear on this site. When I post screenshots, every name and address in them will be made up.

t: A countdown sign for bus stops, built from a $32 board
s: Commercial e-paper bus stop signs cost thousands of dollars each. I'm building a single-stop prototype around a $32 e-paper board and a long-range radio.
x: "When is the bus coming?" is the question every rider has. A sign at the stop that counts down the minutes answers it without a phone. You can try an on-screen version of the sign fed by made-up buses. The price of the off-the-shelf answer The commercial e-paper signs I priced ran roughly $3,500 to $5,000 each, plus a monthly fee of about $50 to $150 per screen. Multiply that by a system's worth of stops and it never gets past a budget meeting. What the sign has to be I wrote the requirements before I looked at parts. - A screen at least 4 inches by 2 inches. - No more than 1.25 inches deep. - Fully enclosed against weather. - Battery powered, because most stops have no electricity. The parts - An Elecrow CrowPanel, which is an ESP32-S3 board with a 5.79 inch e-paper screen built in. About $32. - An RFM95W LoRa radio on 915 MHz. LoRa sends tiny messages over long distances on very little power, and a countdown is a tiny message. - A rechargeable LiPo battery. - Code written in Arduino. E-paper matters here. It only uses power when the picture changes, and it's readable in direct sun, which is where bus stops are. The idea I talked myself out of For a while I thought the answer was a jailbroken Kindle. It's cheap and it has a good screen. It also has the wrong shape and no weatherproofing, and it would be a support headache forever. I dropped it. Where it stands This one is in progress. The plan is a single working stop first, fed by the live vehicle positions feed. Once one sign is working at one stop, I'll write up the build properly.

t: A wizard that fills out the procurement forms
s: A single-page tool that asks plain questions about a purchase and produces the right determination form, with the checks that are easy to forget.
x: Buying things with public money comes with paperwork, and it should. The trouble is that the right form depends on the dollar amount, and each form has checks that are easy to miss when you only do one every few months. You can try a demo of the wizard. It produces a simplified sample form, and nothing you type leaves your browser. What it does The tool is one HTML file. You open it, answer questions in plain language and get a finished form to print. For our purchases it covers two levels. - Micro-purchases, up to $15,000. It produces our Form B-1, which documents that the price is fair and reasonable. - Small purchases, up to $60,000. It produces our Form B-2, which needs three quotes and a record of who was asked and what they offered. At every level it prompts for the SAM.gov check, which confirms a vendor isn't barred from federal work. It also records the DBE status of each offeror, which we track for disadvantaged business participation. Those thresholds and form names are ours. Yours will differ, so treat this as a description of a tool and not as procurement advice. Why a wizard and not a template A blank template assumes you remember the rules. A wizard asks. If the amount crosses a threshold, the questions change. If you list two quotes where three are needed, it tells you before you print, not after an audit. What I left out on purpose There are more forms for larger and more unusual purchases. I started with the two we use most. The rest can wait until the first two have proved themselves. What I'd tell another agency Pick the form people dread most and start there. One form that gets done right the first time is a better argument than any presentation.

t: Color a bus, then watch it save the day
s: A printable coloring page and a small story app that puts a kid's own hand-colored bus into an adventure, ending with a certificate.
x: Outreach to kids usually means a coloring sheet and a sticker. I wanted the coloring sheet to go somewhere. Step one is paper It starts with a printable page, regular letter size. It shows a bus from the side and from the front, with blanks for the artist's name, the bus's name and its route. Kids color it however they like. Step two is the story We scan the page and load it into a small web app, which is a single file like most of what I build. The kid's bus, exactly as they colored it, becomes the hero of a story. It travels five routes, and each route has a problem that the bus solves once the kid answers a trivia question. The kid can also take a selfie, and the app turns it into a comic-book version of their face so they appear in the story next to their bus. At the end it prints a certificate naming them an Honorary Transit Hero. The filter took the longest The comic filter was the stubborn part. My first try found the outlines and flattened the colors in a single pass, and real photos came out blotchy. The fix was to split the work in two. The outlines come from the sharp original photo, which keeps eyes and glasses crisp. The colors come from a gently blurred copy, which calms down skin tones before they're flattened to a few shades. One rule I never bent: the kid's bus artwork is never filtered. It's cropped and nothing else. Their art appears exactly as they made it. Why it's worth doing A kid who has named a bus and watched it save the day looks at the real ones differently. So do their parents.

t: A free week of sailing lessons every June
s: I'm the commodore of our local yacht club, and every June we teach people to sail for free. Here's what the week is and why we do it.
x: I'm the commodore of our local yacht club. That sounds grander than it is. We're a small, democratic sailing club on a lake. The best thing we do all year is the learn-to-sail week. What it is Every June, in the second week of the month, the club runs a week of sailing lessons. It's free. You don't need a boat and you don't need to have ever been on one. Bring a life jacket and we'll handle the rest. We teach on Sunfish. A Sunfish is about fourteen feet of fiberglass with one sail and one rope to worry about. It's simple enough to learn in a week and fast enough that people race them at a world championship level. That's a rare combination. The basics Sailing comes down to a short list, and a week is enough to get comfortable with it. - Where the wind is coming from, which is the whole game. - How to steer with a tiller, which works backwards from what your hands expect. - How to trim the sail. - How to tack, which is turning the front of the boat through the wind. Why it's free Sailing has a reputation for being expensive and closed off. A small club is the opposite of that. The boats belong to the club, I'm one of the teachers and the lake is right there. The only thing between most people and sailing is that nobody ever invited them. So we invite them. Some people come back and join. Some go home with one good week on the water. Both count. Why I keep doing it The best part of the week is watching someone who was nervous at the start sail a boat by themselves at the end. That doesn't wear off, however many times I see it.

t: How to score a race when the boats don't match
s: Club races put fast boats and slow boats on the same course. The Portsmouth yardstick is the simple math that makes it fair.
x: At a small club you race whatever shows up. I sail a Flying Scot, which is a nineteen foot boat with a crew. Next to me on the start line there might be a Sunfish with one person on it. The Scot is faster, so the first boat across the line tells you very little about who sailed best. The yardstick The Portsmouth yardstick fixes this with one number per type of boat. A slower boat gets a higher number. After the race you take each boat's time and correct it. Corrected time is the elapsed time, multiplied by 100, divided by the boat's Portsmouth number. The lowest corrected time wins. A made-up example Say a Flying Scot carries a number of about 90 and a Sunfish about 100. - The Scot finishes in 45 minutes. 45 times 100, divided by 90, is 50 minutes. - The Sunfish finishes in 49 minutes. 49 times 100, divided by 100, is 49 minutes. The Sunfish crossed the line four minutes later and won by a minute. The number says a well-sailed Sunfish should take about eleven percent longer than a well-sailed Scot. This Sunfish took less than that, so it sailed the better race. Score your own race Put in each boat's Portsmouth number and elapsed time. The calculator starts with the example above. For real scoring, use the current numbers from US Sailing's Portsmouth tables. The two here are round numbers for the example. What it's like in practice I scored one of our club races this way, with some help from Claude. I finished third on corrected time. I mention that only to show the math doesn't play favorites with whoever is running it. What the number can't do The yardstick assumes average conditions. In very light wind or a real blow, some boats do better than their number says. There are wind-adjusted versions of the numbers for that. For a weeknight club race, the plain number is close enough and nobody has to argue past dinner. Why I like it It means anyone can race. You don't need the same boat as everyone else. You need a boat, a start line and somebody willing to do a little division afterward.

t: F1 wings for a two-seat go-kart
s: River loves Formula 1, so the Thunder Kart I'm rebuilding is getting a front wing, a rear wing and sidepods. Plywood, PVC pipe and about $50.
x: I'm rebuilding a two-seat Thunder Kart for River. He loves Formula 1 and he loves Red Bull, so a plain go-kart was never going to be enough. It needs wings. The rules I set - Cheap. I already had quarter-inch plywood and half-inch PVC pipe. - No welding and no drilling into the frame. Everything clamps on with U-bolt conduit clamps and comes off again. - Room for my knees. It's a two-seater and I ride along, so the front wing has to stay open on the sides. Front wing A flat center section 18 inches wide sits over the front axle. Two outer sections, 8 inches each, angle down about 15 degrees, with tapered end plates standing up at the tips. The open sides that clear my knees end up making it look more like a real F1 nose, not less. Rear wing This is the showpiece. It has two elements, like the real thing: a main plane 22 inches wide and a smaller flap about an inch and a half above it. They sit on two PVC uprights that lean forward like swan necks, between tall end plates that taper from back to front. Sidepods Flat plywood panels along each side with a scoop shape at the front. They do nothing for airflow. They do a great deal for looking fast while parked. The finish Everything gets sanded, then finished in matte black paint and carbon fiber heat shrink wrap. A heat gun pulls the wrap tight, and from a few feet away it reads as carbon fiber. The bill About $50 in new parts: clamps, a little more pipe, fittings, brackets, sandpaper and two cans of paint. The plywood, the pipe and the wrap were already in the garage. Does any of this make it faster No. At go-kart speeds a plywood wing is a decoration. But a kid who sees his kart with a rear wing on it doesn't need a wind tunnel to know it's faster. I'll post pictures as the build comes together.

t: Formula 1 keeps showing up in everything I build
s: A kart racer, a go-kart with wings and a Grand Prix hidden inside a bus simulator. A short tour of how one kid's favorite sport took over my projects.
x: River loves Formula 1. He loves Red Bull in particular. I didn't plan for that to shape what I build, but look at the evidence. Exhibit one: the kart racer Sloth Rocket Grand Prix is a kart racing game with five themes: F1, rockets, pirates, libraries and sloths. The F1 part was not up for debate. It takes Xbox controllers and a steering wheel with pedals, and four people can race on one screen. Exhibit two: the real kart The two-seat go-kart in our garage is getting a front wing, a two-element rear wing and sidepods. I wrote up the wing build separately. It already has a Red Bull seat. Exhibit three: a Grand Prix inside a bus simulator This is the one I can't defend. I'm building a driving game set on our real bus routes for work. It now contains a five-lap street circuit along the lakefront, an F1-style car, the five red lights at the start and a podium at the end. What the sport is good for F1 is a great way into engineering for a kid. Every question leads somewhere real. - Why do the cars have wings? Because the air pushes them down onto the track. - Why do they change tires? Because grip wears out. - Why did that car slow down? Because someone made a decision about fuel, tires or risk. None of it feels like a lesson, because there's a race on. What's next More of the same, I expect. If you have a kid who is obsessed with something, my advice is to build toward it. You'll never have a more motivated tester.

t: Comics and picture books starring River
s: Two picture books about our family and a three-part space comic that sneaks in relativity and quantum mechanics.
x: Not everything I make for River is a game. Some of it is paper. Two picture books River's Big Day is about one big morning at our house. Rachelle wakes everyone up. The dog does zoomies. There are peanut butter waffles and an episode of Bluey. Then the whole family does the Thriller dance, because that's what we do. River Goes to NASA follows the family on a trip to Space Center Houston. We see Mission Control, the Saturn V at Rocket Park, a moon rock and a model of Starship. River falls asleep in the car on the way home, then tells the dog all about it. Both are written to be read out loud, with big type, short pages and a note on each page describing the picture that goes with it. The details are what make them work. A book about a kid is fine. A book about your kid, your dog and your waffles is a different thing entirely. The comic The bigger project is a space adventure comic in three parts, about forty pages in all. River is the hero, with two companions named Zib and Luma. It's a physics comic in disguise. The story runs on real ideas from relativity and quantum mechanics, pitched so a kid can follow the adventure and a grown-up can notice what's being taught. Part three is called The Race and the Twins. The art is being redone now. When it's finished I'm having it printed locally, so it's a real book on a real shelf. How AI fits in I'm not an illustrator. A few years ago that would have been the end of it. Now I can write the story, describe every panel and work through the art until the pages match what was in my head. The ideas and the family jokes are ours. The typing and the drawing got a lot of help.

t: How this site got built
s: A domain, a free host, no framework and four rounds of me saying "I don't like it yet." Notes on building r3ai.dev with Claude.
x: This site exists because I asked a question about a go-kart game. I'd asked Claude to build a kart racer for River. Then I asked where I could put it so we could play it on the Xbox. A few questions later I owned a domain. The name R cubed is Robert, Rachelle and River. I wanted something short that said both "family" and "AI". r3ai.dev was available and cheap, so that was that. How it's put together - The domain is registered with Cloudflare, and Cloudflare hosts the site. - The source lives on GitHub. When a change is pushed there, the live site updates about a minute later. - There's no framework. A small build script turns plain text files into pages. A post is a text file with a title at the top. - The games are single HTML files that sit beside the pages. I described what I wanted in plain language. Claude wrote the code, tested it and published it. Four rounds of design The first version was plain, and I said so. The second was full glass with every color at once, and I didn't like that either. The third was calm and warm, and then I second-guessed it. The fourth is this one: blues and greens, the colors I keep coming back to, with glass you can see the water through. I'm telling you this because it's the real process. You don't need to know what you want up front. You need to know what you don't like when you see it, and be willing to say so. The showing off A few things here are newer than they need to be. - The background is a small shader that moves like slow water. - The navigation bar bends what's behind it, like real glass, in browsers that support it. - The cube on the home page spins when you drag it. - Page titles slide into place when you move between pages. Everything still works without them. The one thing that went wrong The site went live and I couldn't open it. My phone could. My computer couldn't. The culprit was my home router, which had looked for the site before it existed and kept insisting it still didn't. It caught up on its own.

t: 27 ways I actually use AI
s: A list of every kind of thing I have used AI for, at work and at home, with a short post on each. Start here.
x: People ask me what I actually use AI for. The honest answer is "almost everything, a little." That is not helpful to someone who has never tried it. So I asked Claude to go back through our work together and list every kind of thing we have done. It came back with 27. Each one is now its own short post, built around a real example. These are about how I use AI. For the tools and games themselves, see the project write-ups on the At work and At home pages. How to read these Pick the one closest to your own life. Each post follows the same pattern: what the situation was, what I asked, what came back and where it fell short. I kept that last part in every post on purpose. If you only read one, read When the AI is wrong, and when it says no. At work I manage a City Transit division. Most of this is the unglamorous part of the job. - Getting a straight answer on a regulation - A sanity check before you call the attorney - Turning what you see in the field into a business case - Asking AI what a document is missing - Everyday email: tone, humor and the question you forgot to answer - Writing a careful public reply - Checklists, flyers and forms in an afternoon - Building a procedure library and closing audit findings - Untangling grant money before a deadline - Turning a policy into a tool - A consultant-grade plan from documents already on hand - Building the case for a new service, then rebuilding it - Preparing for a hard meeting in an hour - Checking the numbers before you reply - Building custom software without being a professional developer - Organizing the work itself - Community partnerships and a coloring app - When the AI is wrong, and when it says no At home - Building games for my kid - A hometown bus simulator from real map data - A father-son comic book about physics - Standing up a website in a weekend - Pure fun: a goat racer trailer and texts to my dad - Small life questions - Hobbies and volunteering: sailing scores and a club website - Chasing a big idea, and letting AI poke holes in it - Following curiosity into hard math What I left out Anything that is not mine to share. That means personnel matters, legal matters and anything that should come from the City itself. Two of the work posts come from situations like that. I wrote those with the details removed and kept only the method. How these posts were written Claude drafted all of them from the record of our conversations, in my voice. The examples are real. If something reads wrong, that is on me to fix, and I will. Nothing here is an official statement from my employer.

t: Getting a straight answer on a regulation
s: Four small federal funding and accessibility questions that can each eat an afternoon, and how I ask them now.
x: A lot of my week is small questions with big rulebooks behind them. None of them is hard. Each one can eat an afternoon of searching circulars. The questions Here are four real ones I asked Claude in a single month: - Can federal transit formula funds pay for holiday lighting? - Is there a federal rule against playing music on a fixed-route bus? - How high should the opening of a wastebasket be when I mount one on a bus shelter? - Can a paratransit van bought with grant money make a run to the post office? What came back Each answer came with the reasoning and the citations, which is the part I care about. - Holiday lighting. No rule names it. But federal transit law pays for functional improvements and excludes the added cost of purely decorative elements, so seasonal lighting lands on the wrong side of the line. The answer ended with a suggestion to get that in writing from our regional office, for the audit file. - Music. No federal prohibition. It is a local policy call. The catches are that stop announcements still have to be heard, operator distraction belongs in the safety plan, and music has to be licensed. - The wastebasket. This is my favorite, because the honest answer was "I could not find a transit-specific height." Claude said so, then gave me the general accessibility reach range and the rule about objects sticking out into a walkway, and told me which section of the circular to read myself. - The van. The "revenue vehicle" label is mostly a reporting and inventory concept, not a ban on every other use. The real reasons to send a support vehicle instead are practical: extra miles, shorter useful life and one less van for riders. Where it falls short It can be wrong, and it sometimes cannot open the document it is citing. I treat an answer as a map to the right section, then I read that section. For anything that touches money, I still ask the funding agency. Try it Ask the question the way you would ask a colleague, and add "cite the regulation and tell me what you could not verify." --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: A sanity check before you call the attorney
s: A church invited us to bring a bus to a community event. I used AI to understand the question before I took it to legal.
x: A church invited us to bring a bus to a community event so kids and families could climb aboard and learn how transit works. It sounded like a good day out. It also sounded like the kind of thing a public agency should think about for a minute before saying yes. What I asked I pasted in the invitation and asked whether taking part would create a legal or ethical problem for a public transit agency. What came back A clear framework instead of a yes or no: - The activity itself is secular. We would be showing people a bus. - The event was open to the general public. - No public money would go to the institution. - The real risk is not showing up at a church. The risk is inconsistency: saying yes to one group and no to a similar one. So the test is whether we would do the same thing for any community group, religious or not, that asked the same way. It then recommended something I would not have thought of on my own. Send a short note to the city attorney's office before committing. Partly to confirm there is no local policy I had missed, and partly so there is a record that I checked. Why this matters I used to be a paralegal, so I know how much an attorney's time is worth. The AI did not replace the attorney. It let me walk in with a specific question and the facts already organized, so the conversation is short. Where it falls short It does not know your city's policies unless you give them to it, and it is not your lawyer. Use it to get your question in order. Let counsel make the call. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Turning what you see in the field into a business case
s: We keep meeting riders we cannot talk to. Here is how a real problem at the bus door became a funding memo Finance could approve.
x: More of our riders speak little or no English than a few years ago. There is no interpreter standing by, and a bus on a tight schedule cannot wait for one. My staff and I have been at the door for those conversations. I had an idea for a low-cost fix: City-issued phones paired with earbuds that translate a live conversation. Finance asked for a written description of the business need before any purchase. What I asked I described what we were seeing and asked for a justification memo. What came back, and what I sent back The first draft was correct and lifeless. It had the right legal backbone: federal civil rights law requires agencies like ours to give meaningful access to people with limited English, and the federal guidance uses a four-factor test where cost against resources is one of the factors. A cheap tool that works is exactly what that factor is asking for. But it read like a compliance filing. I told Claude I wanted it to sound like the people who had stood at that bus door. The next version kept the citations and told the story. It also caught things I needed to know before I hit send: - Which phone models the translation feature needs. - That one of the languages our riders speak is not supported by the earbud feature, so the request should be framed as phone-based language help with the earbuds as the hands-free part. - That "allowable" and "reimbursable" are not the same word. It looked for local language data too, and told me plainly when a document it wanted returned an error. Where it falls short It will write the safe version unless you ask for your own voice. I edited the draft myself and handed it back for another pass. Try it Give it the story first, then ask for the rule that supports it. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Asking AI what a document is missing
s: I had a morning meeting about an old scope of work for a backup generator. I asked one question: what is wrong with this, and what is not in it?
x: I inherited a scope of work for a backup generator at our transit facility. It was a few years old, and I had a meeting about it the next morning. I had a feeling it was incomplete. A feeling is not something you can bring to your director. What I asked I uploaded the scope and asked Claude to review it for errors and gaps. What came back Two lists. Problems inside the document: - A cost estimate that was years out of date. - The wrong division listed as the project owner. - A header on the cost sheet that belonged to a different building. - A generator size chosen before anyone had studied the electrical load. - A line item that looked like it came from a different project. - Small arithmetic inconsistencies. Things that were not in the document at all: - Our parking lot drains run straight to the lake next door, which matters a great deal if you are storing fuel. - We are downtown, so there is a noise ordinance to meet. - A generator on an open slab is exposed to weather and theft. - Nobody had compared fuel types. - Permits, and room to grow if we ever charge electric buses. Some of those I already suspected. What the AI did was turn my worries into an organized list I could hand to someone. It then wrote a one-page memo with a fuel comparison table and four next steps. It left me one question in the draft: where is the money coming from? The answer changes which federal requirements apply. Where it falls short Documents age, and people do good work with the information they have at the time. The AI does not know that history. It also cannot see your site. The best findings came from combining what it read with what I know from walking the lot. Try it Upload the document and ask: "What is wrong here, and what should be here that is not?" --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Everyday email: tone, humor and the question you forgot to answer
s: I asked AI to make two emails funnier. It did, and it also noticed that one of them never answered the question I was asked.
x: Not everything I use AI for is serious. Some of it is email, and some of that email is jokes. The PDF master A colleague sent three separate image files where one combined PDF would have done. I drafted a mock-serious reply in character as a "7th degree PDF master" passing an ancient art down to an apprentice. I asked Claude to punch it up. It added a subject line, a line about the rigor of the training ("Select All" and "Print to PDF" both featured), and a new title for me: Keeper of the Sacred Merge. It also gave me a shorter version, in case the long one was too much. The reply that never answered the question The second email taught me more. I had used the wrong accounting code on a requisition, and our purchasing office asked which code I meant to use. I wrote a funny reply and asked Claude to improve it. Before it touched a joke, it pointed out three things: - My reply never said which code to use, which was the only thing I had been asked. - I had mentioned an approval that was not final yet, which could cause the requisition to be held. - One of my jokes had a geography fact wrong. It also reminded me that email at a public agency is a public record, so a joke at a colleague's expense should be made on purpose or not at all. Then it made the email funnier. It told me which jokes it had added so I could cut any that went too far. What I take from this An editor who reads for the point first and the polish second is worth having, even for a two-paragraph email. Where it falls short Humor is personal. Its jokes are not always mine, and I delete some. The voice has to stay yours or people can tell. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Writing a careful public reply
s: When a resident asks whether a rumor is true, the wording matters. Here is how I draft those replies, including the time the AI got ahead of the facts.
x: A resident wrote in because a rider had heard that one of our services might change hands, and the rider was worried. Nothing had been decided. That is exactly the kind of message where a careless sentence becomes a commitment. What I asked I asked for a reply that was honest and reassuring: the City has looked at options, nothing has been decided, and any change would go through the City's normal procurement process and the City Council. What came back Two versions, a short one and a fuller one. I picked the short one. The first drafts also contained a mistake. Claude wrote as if a provider had already been chosen and a purchasing method selected. Neither was true. I said so, and it corrected the draft at once. I mention this because it is the most important lesson in the post: the AI will sometimes treat something you are exploring as something you have decided. In a public reply, that is the error that matters most. It then drafted a cover note sending the reply to our public information officer for review before anything went out. That is our process, and the draft followed it. A second example A community group asked my director for a guest speaker, and she passed the request to me. Claude's first draft wrote to the group as though they had contacted me. They had not. They had never heard of me. The second draft introduced me, explained how the request reached me, and then said yes. What I take from this Tell it who is writing to whom, and what each person already knows. That context is the difference between a reply that sounds right and one that reads as slightly off. Where it falls short It does not know what has been decided and what has not. You do. Read every public-facing sentence as if it will be quoted back to you. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Checklists, flyers and forms in an afternoon
s: Cleaning checklists, a fare flyer, a staff reference sheet, a fillable form and an anonymous suggestion box. None of it is glamorous. All of it used to wait.
x: Every workplace has a pile of small documents nobody has time to make. This is where AI has saved me the most hours with the least drama. What I have made this way - A daily bus cleaning checklist for our custodian. One page is a grid: a column per bus, a row per task, and room to mark done, not applicable or problem. The second page is a work log with signature lines. - A building cleaning checklist to match it. I uploaded the bus checklist and asked for the same look. Claude opened the original file, read the exact fonts and colors out of it, and matched them. When I asked for a revision, it split the document in two: one for the inside of the building, room by room, and one for the outside areas with morning and afternoon columns. - A "show your ID" flyer for discounted fares, half a letter page, first in portrait and then in landscape when I changed my mind. - A one-page staff sheet on what to do when a paratransit rider moves here from another city, with the regulation cited at the bottom. - A fillable PDF that my director asked me to complete on behalf of the division. Claude filled it in from the division's point of view, and then listed the questions it was not comfortable answering for me. - An anonymous suggestion box built on the form tool we already pay for, with a QR code to post around the office. The detail that mattered On the suggestion box, Claude pointed out that our form tool records who is responding by default for work accounts. You have to switch that off, or "anonymous" is not anonymous. That one note is the difference between a tool people trust and one they do not. Where it falls short It makes assumptions to fill gaps, such as which rooms are locked or how many restrooms are outside. The good news is that it lists those assumptions at the end. Read that list. It is always the most useful paragraph. Try it Upload a document you already like and say "make me another one in this style for a different job." --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Building a procedure library and closing audit findings
s: A federal review left us with findings and a deadline. Here is how AI helped turn scattered old documents into procedures we can actually follow.
x: Every few years the federal agency that funds transit reviews agencies like ours top to bottom. Ours produced findings, each with a corrective action and a deadline. Findings are mostly about paper. Is the procedure written down, is it current, and can you show that you follow it? Some of ours needed updating. What I used AI for - Corrective action documents across five finding areas. - A written procedure library, built one document at a time with a consistent numbering scheme and the same layout throughout. The complaint procedure and the operator training manual are finished. - A retraining plan on serving riders with disabilities, with a workbook to track who has completed what. - A paratransit eligibility packet: the application, a rider's guide and a fillable acceptance letter. - A revised asset management plan and the access request forms for a federal system. How the work actually goes The pattern is the same each time. I upload the old document, the finding and the regulation. Claude drafts. I correct what it got wrong about how we really operate. It redrafts. What surprised me is how often it stops to ask. For our administrative procedures it gave me a twelve-part information request before it would write a word, because it did not have the facts. Another procedure sat unfinished until I could supply details that only I had. An assistant that will not invent your procedures for you is the kind you want near an audit. Where it falls short It can write a procedure that reads well and does not match what your staff do on a Tuesday morning. A written procedure you do not follow is worse than none. I read every draft against real practice. It also needs real data. Our safety plan update could not be finished until we had actual incident numbers. It did not guess at them. Try it Start with one finding. Give the AI the finding, the rule and your current document, and ask what is missing. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Untangling grant money before a deadline
s: Several older grants, a handful of invoices and a date after which the money goes away. AI did the matching and found the invoices that did not fit.
x: Federal grants come with a period of performance. When it ends, what you have not drawn down is gone. I had several older grants closing on the same date and a few vendor invoices to match against them. The puzzle Each grant is divided into budget lines by category: bus stops and stations, support equipment and so on. An invoice can only be charged where the category matches and there is room left. So the question is never just "do we have the money." It is "do we have the money in the right line of the right grant." What I asked I gave Claude the remaining balance on each line of each grant, and the invoices, and asked what could be drawn from where. What came back A walk through each grant and each line. The useful part was what did not fit. One invoice was larger than the room left in its category across all of the grants. Two others were far too large for theirs. Claude did not force them in. It said they probably belonged to a different grant, pointed to which one, and asked a question I should have asked first: is it the full invoice that gets drawn, or only the federal share? That did not solve my problem. It told me exactly what my problem was, before I submitted a draw that would have been rejected. Where it falls short It only knows the balances I give it. If my figures are stale, the answer is stale. It is not looking at the federal system. I am. I would also never let it submit anything. It does the arithmetic and the matching, and I check the result against the live system and make the draw myself. Try it Put your balances and invoices in a table and ask "what fits where, and what does not fit anywhere?" --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Turning a policy into a tool
s: I wanted to save our purchasing staff some work on small purchases. That turned into a memo, then a form, then a wizard that writes the paperwork.
x: Small purchases create a surprising amount of paperwork. Federal rules let agencies like ours buy low-cost items without competitive quotes, as long as the price is reasonable and documented. But each request still adds work for our purchasing staff. I wanted to give them one clear document showing the authority for these purchases, so they would have less to review. Step one: the memo I asked Claude for a memo laying out the federal and local authority for small purchases, including from online retailers. Step two: stop and read the real policy Before it revised anything, I told it to wait until I could upload the City's actual procurement procedures. I am glad I did. The first draft was built from federal rules, and the local policy differs in ways that matter: - Our ceiling for the next tier of purchases is much lower than the federal one. - Three quotes are always required at that tier. - A check against the federal list of barred vendors is required at every dollar amount, even the smallest. On that last point Claude had told me earlier that the check only applied above a certain amount. When it read our policy, it said it had been wrong and corrected the memo. Step three: the form, then the tool Next came a price determination form that matches the one in our procedures. Then came the part I like most: a small web page that asks questions about a purchase, one at a time, and produces the right completed form at the end. That is the jump worth noticing. A policy is something people have to read. A tool is something people can just use. I describe the tool itself in A wizard that fills out the procurement forms. Knowing when to stop Claude offered to extend the wizard to four more forms. I said no. I want to live with the first two before building more. Where it falls short It will write from general rules if that is all it has. Your local policy is the one that counts, so give it the document. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: A consultant-grade plan from documents already on hand
s: A consultant asked for our transit plan. We did not have a stand-alone one. Here is how the documents we did have became a 14-page plan.
x: A consultant working on a state road study asked for our current transit planning documents. We had a safety plan, the regional transportation plan and years of operating records. We did not have a single stand-alone transit plan to hand over. What I asked First, I asked Claude to check whether we had already covered these documents in earlier conversations. Then I asked it to build a transit plan from the sources we had, and to make it look like something a consulting firm would produce. What came back A 14-page, print-ready plan: - A cover page. - Charts of ridership and operations: five donut charts, two bar charts and a trend line. - A schematic of the route network. - An organization chart. - A diagram showing how the plan fits under the regional and state plans. - A phased roadmap. Everything in it came from documents we already had on file. Nothing was invented. Where the sources did not say something, the plan did not say it. Two rounds of revision I asked for more visual polish, and then for a change in how one future service was presented. Each time I got a complete new file back, not a list of edits to make myself. The part I did myself The plan mentions a service we are still evaluating. Anything that sounds like a commitment about timing needs to be read by our legal and public information staff before it leaves the building. Claude had that note from me and kept the language conditional. The review itself is still a job for people. Where it falls short A plan assembled from existing documents is only as current as those documents. It is a faithful summary, not new analysis. If you need new analysis, you still need a study. Try it Gather what you already have, upload it, and ask for one document that tells the whole story with sources. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Building the case for a new service, then rebuilding it
s: I spent weeks on a presentation about on-demand transit. Then one of my assumptions turned out to be wrong, and the whole thing had to be rebuilt as something else.
x: I was asked to look into on-demand transit: collect the information, visit a city that already runs it, and come back with a report for City leadership. To be clear about where things stand: no decision has been made. The City has reviewed options, and anything further goes through the City's procurement process and the City Council. This post is about the work of preparing the report. What we built Over one long conversation, Claude and I produced: - A presentation built from my source material and revised through seven major versions. - Print handouts that match it, with page numbers. - A full script, written and rewritten. - Emails to the people I needed answers from. - Research into state purchasing law and federal procurement rules. I visited another city to see eighteen months of their results in person. Those numbers went into the deck the same week. Then it changed Partway through, I learned that the purchasing approach I had assumed was not available to us. The report could no longer be a pitch for one arrangement. It had to become a neutral look at the service model itself. That meant rebuilding it. Company-specific figures came out. The framing changed from "here is a partnership" to "here is what we learned and what the options are." Claude redid the deck, the script and the handouts to match, and I asked it to keep the tone forward-looking. A plan that changes is not a plan that failed. What I take from this Before AI, a change like that would have meant starting the slides over. This time it was a rework, not a restart. The cost of being wrong got smaller, and that makes it easier to do the right thing when the facts change. Where it falls short It got a point of state law wrong, with confidence. I caught it. I wrote about that in When the AI is wrong, and when it says no. It also offered me a condensed version of the report when I wanted the full one. You have to say what you want. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Preparing for a hard meeting in an hour
s: I had a disagreement over how a written policy should be read, and a meeting in sixty minutes. I asked AI to argue the other side.
x: I am keeping the details out of this one, because they are not mine to share. The method is the useful part. I disagreed with another office about how a written policy should be read. I had the policy in front of me, and I thought the text supported my reading. I had a meeting within the hour. What I asked I did not ask "am I right?" I asked: what will the other side say, and in what order? What came back A ranked list of the arguments I was likely to hear, each with the strongest version of it. Some of them were good arguments. A few I had not considered at all: - Questions about what a key word in the policy actually means. - Practical concerns about coverage on a small team. - The worry about precedent: if this is allowed here, who asks next? - The mechanics of making it work in the systems we already use. Then three pieces of advice: - Bring a plan that answers the practical concern before anyone raises it. - Know one specific fact cold before walking in, because the whole question could turn on it. - Close by asking which written provision supports the other reading. That last one is a question, not an argument. It keeps the conversation on the text. What I take from this Before the meeting, I had also drafted three emails with Claude's help: a detailed one, a softer one, and a short note asking to talk in person. The short note mattered most to me. I would rather settle things at the lowest level, face to face, than win an email thread. The point of the preparation is not to be more combative. When you have already heard the other side's best points, you can listen when they make them. Where it falls short It only knows the documents you show it. It cannot tell you about the history between two offices or what was said in a hallway. And it should never be the one deciding. It helps you think. You go to the meeting. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Checking the numbers before you reply
s: Someone sent me a total. Before I agreed or disagreed, I had AI read the rulebook and recount.
x: This is another one where the details stay out. The habit is what I want to pass on. I received an email with a number in it: a count of how many times something had happened. The number was the basis for what the email wanted done next. My first instinct was to reply to the request. What I did first I uploaded two things: the written policy that defines how those events are counted, and the spreadsheet of the underlying records. I asked Claude to count them according to the policy. What came back A different number. The reason was not carelessness on anyone's part. It was a definition. The policy groups related entries into a single event. The total I had been sent counted each entry separately. A second category of entries fell under a different section of the policy altogether. Claude showed its work row by row, so I could check the count myself. I did. What I did with it Here is the part I think matters. I did not open my reply with "your number is wrong." The underlying concern in the email was fair, and I agreed with it. I wrote a cooperative reply, went ahead with the right next step, and used neutral wording that did not depend on any particular total. The recount was for my own understanding. Knowing the real number changed how I wrote, not whether I cooperated. What I take from this Two things: - Read the definition before you accept the total. Most number disputes are definition disputes. - Being right about a detail is not a reason to make a colleague wrong in writing. Where it falls short A spreadsheet has to be read correctly, and an AI can misread a column. Ask it to show each row it counted and why. If it cannot show its work, do not use the number. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Building custom software without being a professional developer
s: I taught myself to build web pages. With AI doing a large share of the typing, I now build the tools my division needs when nothing off the shelf fits.
x: I am not a software engineer. I taught myself web development because the tools I needed either did not exist or cost more than a small transit system can pay. What I have built - A driver scheduling system with a dispatch board that runs in a browser. - A paratransit scheduling app. - A live feed of bus locations in the standard format that trip-planning apps read. - A bus stop arrival display, still a prototype, built on a small e-paper board. - A purchasing wizard, which started life as a memo. See Turning a policy into a tool. - An emergency operations portal for coordinating a hurricane shelter: one web page, no installation, built to work on a phone. How it works in practice I describe what I need in plain language. Claude writes the code. I run it, see what is wrong, and say so. We repeat that until it works. The shelter portal shows the part people do not expect. Claude did not just write it. It opened the page in an automated browser at three phone widths, checked all eleven screens for anything that ran off the edge, and found two real layout bugs. It also told me which wide tables were meant to scroll sideways, so I would not mistake them for bugs. It keeps a list of what is not done, too. For the portal: saving your work when the page refreshes, an offline indicator, search on the roster and data export. Why single files Several of these are one HTML file. That is on purpose. A single file can be emailed, opened from a thumb drive and used when the network is down, which is exactly when an emergency tool is needed. Where it falls short - You still have to understand what you are building well enough to test it. - Software that people rely on needs backups, security and someone who will maintain it. AI does not take on that responsibility. I do. - It tells me what it could not test. I take that list seriously. Try it Start with something small that annoys you every week. Describe it the way you would to a new employee. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Organizing the work itself
s: Before my assistant manager and I sat down to sort out everything on our plates, I asked AI how to run that meeting.
x: My assistant manager and I had too many open items and no shared place to keep them. We planned a working session to list everything, rank it and decide who owns what. What I asked How should we organize all of this, using software we already have? What came back A tool recommendation and a meeting plan. The tool was the task board that comes with our office software. No new purchase, no new login. Claude explained when a simple list would be the better choice instead, which told me it was not just naming the first thing that came to mind. The meeting plan was the valuable part: - Write down every open item first. Do not filter and do not debate. - Pull out anything with a deadline that is close or already past. - Group the rest into a handful of themes. - Give each item a simple priority. - Give every item one owner. - Agree on a short, regular check-in so the board stays current. The part that surprised me Because Claude has worked with me on most of these projects, it suggested the groupings itself: grants and compliance, purchasing, technology projects, personnel, budget and reporting. It also pointed out that two items had outside deadlines that had already passed, and said those should be handled first in the meeting, not filed with the backlog. It offered to fill in a starter board so the two of us could react to something instead of facing a blank page. That is a good trick for any meeting. I am also building a workbook to track our goals for the year the same way. Where it falls short A board only works if two people keep it up. No software fixes that. And its picture of my workload is only as good as what I have told it. One of the "deadlines" it flagged was for a grant we ended up not applying for. Try it Ask for the agenda, not just the tool. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Community partnerships and a coloring app
s: Transit is a public service, and the public should like it. Two small examples of using AI for the community side of the job.
x: Most of this series is about compliance and paperwork. This post is about the part of the job I enjoy most. A follow-up email that sounded like us My assistant manager and I met with someone from a local organization about a grant her group might sponsor: adding art to our bus stop shelters. Public art at a bus stop tells a neighborhood that somebody cares about it. It is an early conversation and nothing is promised. But I wanted the follow-up email to do two things: show how excited we were, and make clear that my assistant manager and I come as a team. I told Claude exactly that. The draft it wrote was warm without being gushing, signed by both of us, and listed three specific things we could help with: grant writing, connections and planning. It also reminded me to add the organization's name and to copy my colleague. Small things, and the kind I forget when I am writing in a hurry. A coloring and story app for riders The other project is one I built: a coloring and story app for community outreach. Kids color a printed bus, and the app makes their own bus the hero of a story. The full write-up is Color a bus, then watch it save the day. It is not complicated software. But a transit system has very little to hand a child, and now we do. With AI doing the typing, it was within reach. Why this belongs in the series People assume AI at work means cutting costs. For me it has mostly meant having time for things that were never going to make the list. Nobody budgets hours for a coloring app. When the hours it takes shrink enough, you can just do it. Where it falls short Enthusiasm in an email has to be real. The AI can match a tone I describe. It cannot supply the feeling. If I had not actually been excited about those shelters, the email would have read as hollow. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: When the AI is wrong, and when it says no
s: The most useful post in this series. The mistakes I caught, the ones I nearly did not, and the requests the AI turned down.
x: If you read one post in this series, read this one. Everything else I have written is about what works. This is about the edges. When it was wrong A point of state law. While I was researching purchasing options, Claude told me with full confidence that a new state law did not cover services. It did. That language had been added during the legislative process. I caught it because I had read the bill. If I had not, the error would have gone into a presentation for City leadership. When I pointed it out, it said plainly that it had been wrong and fixed the work. I still told it, later, that the mistake had cost it some of my trust. It acknowledged that too. Assuming a decision. In a draft reply to a resident, it wrote as if we had chosen a provider and a purchasing method. We had done neither. A wrong first guess. I asked about a scrape on my car. It guessed paint transfer. It was bare plastic, which is a completely different repair. A rule it misstated, then corrected when I uploaded our actual policy. The pattern: it is most often wrong where it is filling a gap with something that sounds likely. When it corrected itself Not every catch was mine. Claude once went back over a report it had written for me, unprompted, and corrected twelve of its own claims. It removed one comparison entirely because newer data no longer supported it. Its own estimate got smaller as a result. When it said no - I asked for a famous actor to appear in a joke movie trailer. It declined, because that would show a real person agreeing to something he had not. When I said he was fine with it, it held its position, politely. - I asked for a jacket logo using a well-known rocket company's name and a job title that does not exist. It declined that too and offered an original design. - I asked it to restart my home router. It would not enter the router's access code, and gave me the steps to do it myself. What I take from this Check anything that matters against the source. Tell it when it is wrong. And notice that an assistant that will tell you no is one whose yes means more. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Building games for my kid
s: I am not a game developer. Here is how one request became a twelve-mission space game with our whole family in it, and what I learned about directing an AI.
x: My son River loves rockets. I wanted to make him a game that knew his name. Play River's Rocket Works, or read what is in it. This post is about how it got made. River's Rocket Works I asked Claude for a rocket-building game in a browser, with two requirements: it had to call River by name, and it had to tell him he is a great rocket engineer. What came back is a 3D game in one file. You pick tanks, engines and boosters, read a flight forecast, and then fly: countdown, staging, orbit, landing, docking. A voice narrates. It works with a controller, a keyboard or a touch screen. Then I kept having ideas, and it grew from seven missions to twelve: - A Moon landing and a Mars rover delivery. - A rover race on Saturn's rings. - A storm rally on Jupiter, with a secret golden tornado. - A wormhole run through an asteroid field. - A race around the solar system starring the whole family. In that last one River rides a star with a rainbow trail. Rachelle rides a unicorn. I drive a Viking ship pulled by two giant goats. Our white Lab, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, competes as herself. I asked for a screen where you can pick any of us, so River does not always have to be River. The praise changes each time he finishes a mission: rocket builder, aerospace designer, mission commander. What I learned about how it works - I gave specific directions, one round at a time. "Slow the ship to three quarters speed" works better than "make it easier." - Claude tested the game by playing it automatically from start to finish. Each time, it told me what it could not test: sound, a real controller and how it looks on a real screen. So I tested those. - One level I had named after a famous movie. Claude renamed it to avoid borrowing someone else's trademark, and kept my jokes. Sloth Rocket Grand Prix The other game is on this site and you can play it now. I wrote about it in its own post. Where it falls short The graphics are simple shapes, not artist-made models. And a game like this is never finished. There is always one more mission to add. Try it Ask your kid what the game should be. Then type exactly what they said. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: A hometown bus simulator from real map data
