s: It started as a toy trolley on a made-up grid. It became a driving game on our real streets, with real routes and tens of thousands of real buildings.
x: This one sits between work and home. I wanted a small driving game where you pilot a trolley around downtown and pick up riders. It did not stay small. What is in the game is covered in A driving game set on our real bus routes. This post is about how it grew. How it grew Version one was a first-person trolley on a made-up grid of streets. Then I asked for our real routes. Claude read the published transit schedule data, the same feed trip-planning apps use, and rebuilt the game around the five actual routes with their real names, colors and stops. Then I asked for the real city. I supplied public map data: streets, addresses, parcels and the city limits. Claude rebuilt the world at true scale with real street names and more than forty thousand building footprints, later filled in with public building datasets. Then we added the fun parts: - A second vehicle, a 35-foot bus, modeled from a photo of the placard and the operator's manual. - Controller support and two-player split screen. - A radio with original music. - A free-drive mode with item crates. The items are local: hot sauce rockets, blue crabs, a crawfish that slows you down and Mardi Gras beads as a shield. - A five-lap grand prix on a real street circuit, with a five-light start and a podium. - Driving physics based on the real weight and power of the vehicles. People who have tried it like it. Somewhere along the way it stopped being a weekend toy and got a proper name: LC Transit Simulator. The data problems were the real work - The first street file only had roads ending in Street, Drive, Road and Lane. No avenues, no boulevards, no highways. We needed a different file. - The big map files were too large to upload in chat. Claude read them straight from my computer instead. - Bus stops first appeared in the middle of the road and had to be moved to the curb. Making it look like home I want the buildings to look real. My first idea was to use online street-level imagery. Claude explained that the terms of service for those services rule that out. The better plan is to film the routes myself with a 360 camera that records GPS. I picked a camera and have filming notes: where to mount it, what time of day and how fast to drive. I have not filmed yet. Where it falls short It is still in progress and not posted here yet. The buildings are plain blocks until the filming is done. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: A father-son comic book about physics
s: River wrote a space adventure about the biggest unsolved problem in physics. We are turning it into a real printed comic book.
x: River loves writing comics. One of his is a space adventure starring himself and two friends named Zib and Luma. The plot is about getting the physics of the very big and the physics of the very small to agree with each other, which is a problem that real physicists have not solved. He wrote it for kids his own age. There is more about it, and the picture books, in Comics and picture books starring River. I decided it deserved to be a real book. What we are making A 40-page educational comic in three parts, printed at standard comic book size by a local print shop. What AI did - Organized the pages into the three parts. - Lettered the pages: the speech balloons and captions. - Wrote a prompt for each page's art, so the look stays consistent from the first page to the last. - Worked out the print side: the page size and the file format a print shop wants, so I do not show up with something they cannot use. What I changed my mind about The first round of artwork looked like it was made by a computer. I did not want that for River's book, across all forty pages. We talked through two options: run the existing images through a filter, or redo the art. I chose to redo it. I am regenerating the art myself in another image tool, one page at a time from the page prompts. After that, the new art gets swapped in and the lettering goes back on top. It is slower. It is also the part River and I do together, which was the point all along. What I take from this AI is good at the scaffolding of a creative project: the page count, the file formats, the consistency and the tedious lettering. The story is River's. The decisions about how it should look are ours. I would not hand those over even if I could. Where it falls short AI-made art still has a look, and readers can tell. Getting past that takes more human effort, not less. If you want a book that feels handmade, plan to put your hands on it. Try it If your kid has a story, ask an AI how many pages it would be and what a printer needs. Seeing that it is possible is half of it. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Standing up a website in a weekend
s: This site is brand new. Here is what I did, what the AI did, and why I could not load my own website the day it went live.
x: You are reading the result of this one. The longer story is in How this site got built. This is the short version, with the lessons. What I wanted One site with two sides: what I build at work and what I build at home. A blog under both. A place to put my games. A name that had something to do with AI, on a domain that was cheap. Picking the name I liked "R cubed" for Robert, Rachelle and River. Claude checked which versions of the name were available across many domain endings in a batch, with prices. I picked r3ai.dev and registered it myself. Building it Claude built the whole site: - A home page, the two sections, a blog and an About page. - A small script that turns plain text files into finished pages, so adding a post means adding one text file. - A feed and a site map. I created the hosting account, connected it and set up the place where the files live. Once those were connected, the site was live. I did not like it The first design was plain. I said so, and asked for something that would look current in 2027: glass effects and modern styling. It took four rounds to get to what you see. Saying "I do not like this" is allowed. It costs one message. My own site would not load Then I could not open the site on my computer at home. My phone could. Claude checked from my computer and found the cause. My home router had looked up the address before the site existed, been told "no such site," and remembered that answer. The site was fine. My router was out of date. The fixes were to wait half an hour, check from my phone on cellular data, or unplug the router and plug it back in. I asked Claude to restart the router for me. It declined, because that meant entering the router's access code, and gave me the steps instead. In the end the router caught up on its own. Where it falls short I still had to make the accounts, pay and approve things. That is as it should be. And a site needs something worth reading, which no tool supplies. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Pure fun: a goat racer trailer and texts to my dad
s: Not everything has to be useful. A 30-second movie trailer made from one photo, and a running joke about my dad's car.
x: Some of what I do with AI has no purpose at all, and I recommend it. The trailer Rachelle and I have a photo of the two of us in a chariot. I asked Claude to turn it into a 30-second movie trailer in which we are goat racers from a rainbow realm. It made a video from that one photo. There were camera moves, title cards and an orchestral score it composed itself. It added a mock rating card. It named our goats after the two goats that pull Thor's chariot in Norse mythology. Then I asked for a "festival cut." That one got galloping unicorns with rainbow trails, lasers and a hawk that screeches. Two things it would not do: - It made up its own festival laurels and would not use a real film festival's name, since we had not been accepted by one. - I asked for a cameo by a famous actor. It declined, because the trailer would show a real person taking part in something he never agreed to. I told it he was fine with it. It said it had no way to know that, and offered to use real footage if I could get any. I got three versions of the trailer and no celebrity. Fair enough. Captain Dashboard My dad needed an address confirmed. I asked Claude to help me reply as a "Supreme AI Overlord" who looks down on his car's navigation system, which we named Captain Dashboard. Claude looked up the address first, so the joke was also correct. My dad signed off his reply in character, and I asked for a comeback. I was not sure which car he would be driving, so Claude wrote one version for each. Why this is in the series Because this is how most people will get comfortable with AI. Nobody learns a tool by reading a manual. You learn it by making something that makes your wife laugh. It also taught me something about how the tool behaves. It will be as silly as I want. It will not pretend a real person said or did something. Where it falls short The video is made by code moving a single photo around. It is charming, and it is not a studio production. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Small life questions
s: A benefits document, a scraped bumper and a strange name on a restaurant. Three everyday questions and what I learned from asking them.
x: These are the questions I would once have typed into a search engine and then given up on after the third ad. Is this term or whole life insurance? I had a document about life insurance through work and could not tell what kind it was. I uploaded it and asked. The answer was group term life, and the useful part was why: - Coverage ends when you leave the job. - The benefit goes down as you get older. - There is an option to convert it, with a 30-day window. - There is no cash value. It then told me to ask HR or the insurer for the certificate of coverage if I wanted it confirmed officially. This is information, not financial advice. Can I fix this bumper myself? Someone hit my car in a parking lot and left. I wanted the cheapest repair I could do myself. Claude's first guess was wrong. It thought the black mark was paint from the other car and suggested polishing it off. I told it the black was the bare plastic of the bumper showing through. That changed the whole answer. The new one was a proper sequence: clean, sand, a special primer that makes paint stick to plastic, color, then clear coat. It included how to spray metallic paint so the flakes lie flat, and a warning about weather. The lesson is that it could not see my car. I could. When I corrected it, the advice got good. What does "three dots and a dash" mean? I saw the phrase and asked. Three dots and a dash is Morse code for the letter V, which stood for victory in the Second World War. Then I mentioned I had seen it as the name of a place in Chicago. It is a tiki bar, named for a cocktail invented to celebrate the end of the war. The drink's garnish is three cherries and a piece of pineapple: three dots and a dash. What I take from this You can ask a follow-up. That is the whole difference from a search engine. The second question is usually where the good answer is. Where it falls short It guesses when it cannot see. Describe the thing carefully, and correct it when it is wrong. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Hobbies and volunteering: sailing scores and a club website
s: I race small sailboats and help run a yacht club. AI now does the race arithmetic and some of the homework a volunteer board never has time for.
x: I sail, I teach a free sailing class every year, and I am the commodore of our local yacht club. Volunteer work is real work with no staff. Scoring a race When different kinds of boats race each other, a fast catamaran and a small single-sail dinghy cannot be compared by the clock alone. Each boat type has a handicap number. You take the elapsed time, multiply by 100 and divide by the boat's number to get a corrected time. I explain the math in How to score a race when the boats don't match. After a club race I gave Claude the elapsed times and boats. It looked up the handicap numbers, did the arithmetic and gave me standings. Then I started reading from the paper score sheet and the corrections began: - One boat had been sailed by one person and not two, which changes its number. - One boat was a different model from the one I had typed. - One elapsed time was off by two minutes. That one was mine. Each time, Claude recalculated and reissued the standings. One boat was not on the standard list at all, so it worked out a number from a different rating system and said clearly that this was derived, not official. A flyer for sailing lessons Claude redesigned the flyer for my summer sailing class over several rounds. Along the way one line changed that should not have: whether life jackets are provided. That is not a design detail. You bring your own. Proofread the facts, not just the layout. Homework for the club website Our club website is old. Before proposing anything to the board, I asked for research on what similar clubs do. The findings: - One software platform is used by most of our peer clubs. - The website and the member portal are one decision, not two. - Our best benefit is barely mentioned anywhere: members can visit dozens of other clubs. When the old site blocked Claude from reading it, it did not ask for a password. It told me how to make my own copy of the site and upload that. Where it falls short It cannot see the score sheet. Every error it fixed was one I had typed. Check the inputs. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Chasing a big idea, and letting AI poke holes in it
s: I have a concept for helping local governments modernize. The most valuable thing AI did was make my own numbers smaller.
x: I have an idea I call Clarus. It is a concept, not a company. I say so out loud whenever I show it to anyone. The idea is a consultancy that helps local governments modernize: review how each department works, find the waste, propose fixes, estimate the savings, and be paid from savings that are actually proven. What I built with AI - A logo, through several rounds, from flat marks to an animated one. - A website mockup that explains the idea, with a calculator for the cost of doing things the old way. - A briefing document that works through public budget documents and estimates what a city could save. Where it got interesting After writing the first draft of the briefing, Claude reviewed its own work without being asked. It corrected twelve of its own claims. Some examples of what changed: - One comparison was dropped because newer data no longer supported it. - One was rebuilt on a fairer baseline, because the original year had been distorted by a hurricane. - One proposed saving was removed entirely, because state law requires the expense. The total estimate went down by about a quarter. A sales pitch that makes its own number smaller is not something I expected, and the document is far more believable for it. The third draft added a section on what the city already does well. That was the right instinct. Nobody wants to read a report that is only about what they are doing wrong. The question I have to answer first Claude also raised something I needed to hear, and raised it more than once. Ethics rules may limit what a public employee can do in business with their own employer. Its advice was to get an opinion from the state ethics board before pitching anything. That is where the idea stands. It is a concept I am developing, and that question comes before any next step. What I take from this Ask the AI to argue against your idea. If it only agrees with you, it is not helping. Where it falls short A savings estimate built from public documents is an outside view. It is a place to start asking questions, not a finding. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Following curiosity into hard math
s: I am not a mathematician. I spent many hours with an AI on one of the most famous unsolved problems anyway.
x: The last post in this series is the least practical one. I have a strong interest in advanced mathematics and no credentials in it. The Riemann Hypothesis is one of the most famous unsolved problems there is. It concerns a pattern in how the prime numbers are spread out. People have been working on it for more than 160 years. What I did Over a long series of conversations, I explored one way of approaching the problem with Claude. The approach comes from the branch of mathematics that studies operators, which is the same toolkit that quantum physics is built on. Let me be plain about the result: I did not solve it. Nobody should read this and think otherwise. So why do it Because I could finally ask. Before this, if I got stuck on page three of a mathematics paper, I stayed stuck. There was nobody to ask what a symbol meant, or why a step followed from the one before it, or whether my idea was new or a well-known dead end. Now there is. I can ask the basic question, and then the next one, and then the next. I can propose something and be told where it breaks. That is what a patient teacher does, and most adults do not have one. What I take from this Learning for its own sake is a good enough reason to use these tools. River wrote a comic about getting the physics of the very big and the very small to agree, so hard questions run in the family. I wrote about that in A father-son comic book about physics. Where it falls short This is where I would be most careful. An AI can make a mathematical argument sound better than it is. It can be agreeable when it should be skeptical. An idea that feels like a breakthrough after midnight should be treated as a guess until someone qualified has checked it. So ask it to find the flaw, not to confirm the idea. And enjoy the learning for what it is. Try it Pick the subject you always wished you understood. Ask the first question you were too embarrassed to ask in school. --- Part of the series 27 ways I actually use AI. Claude drafted this post from the record of our work together.

t: Sloth Rocket Grand Prix: a kart racer in one HTML file
s: I asked an AI for a kart racer themed on Formula 1, rockets, pirates, libraries and sloths. Here is what came back, how to play it and where it falls short.
x: The brief was a go-kart racer in a single HTML file, with five themes that have nothing to do with each other: Formula 1, rockets, pirates, libraries and sloths. I gave that to Claude on a Sunday morning and had a playable game before lunch. Play Sloth Rocket Grand Prix What's in it - Five courses. Pole Position Park, Launch Pad Loop, Cutthroat Cove, The Grand Stacks and Slowpoke Canopy. - Five karts. A formula car, an astronaut on a rocket, a pirate galleon, a librarian's book cart and a sloth on a log. Each one handles differently. - Up to four players on one screen, with computer rivals filling the rest of the grid. - Three levels (Rookie, Pro and Legend) and a five-race Grand Prix with points. - Items. Turbo, cannonball, book trap, heat shield and the sloth spell, which slows down everyone ahead of you. How to play Open the game in Chrome or Edge on a computer. - Xbox controller: press A to join. RT or A accelerates, LT or B brakes, RB drifts, and LB or X uses an item. - Keyboard: press W or the up arrow to join. Steer with WASD or the arrows, drift with Space or Shift, and use items with E or Enter. - Wheel and pedals: press any button on the wheel to join. A short calibration walks through steering, gas and brake. Hold drift through a corner and let go for a boost. Where it falls short - The graphics are simple blocks. There are no artist-made models. - A wheel gets no force feedback, because browsers don't offer it. - I haven't tried it on an Xbox console yet. It should run in the console's Edge browser, but that's a guess until I test it. What I'd like to add More courses, a time trial mode and River's ideas, once he has had a turn at it.

t: What goes in the work section
s: A short note on what I plan to write about from the transit side, and what I'll leave out.
x: This side of the site is for the work I do in public transit, and for the software I build to make that work easier. What to expect - Write-ups of tools I've built, with the problem each one solves. - Notes on using AI for the unglamorous parts of running a transit system. - Things that didn't work, and why. What I'll leave out Anything that isn't mine to share. That covers personnel matters, anything confidential, and anything that should come from the city itself. Nothing here is an official statement from my employer. It's one manager's notes.
